summary: Explains problems that arise when a mobile device that supports both IPv4 and IPv6 must run both Mobile IPv4 and Mobile IPv6. It argues for using a single mobility management protocol and discusses requirements for supporting that. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A phone that uses two different systems to keep track of its location is messy, so this explains why one system would be better.

questions: why not run mobile ipv4 and mobile ipv6 together
subtitle: Why a phone that speaks IPv4 and IPv6 should not need two separate mobility protocols.

tldr.problem: A node that supports both IPv4 and IPv6 needs both Mobile IPv4 and Mobile IPv6 to keep roaming, which means double the signaling, configuration and operation.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the problems of running both protocols side by side and lists work areas that would let one mobility protocol manage both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
tldr.outcome: It recommends extending Mobile IPv6 and Mobile IPv4 so either can handle both address families, without forcing operators to run two protocols at once. It is a problem statement, not a protocol.

facts.label: Signaling per handoff when running both

today: RFC 4977 is an Informational problem statement from August 2007 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out the problem and work areas rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Two Mobility Protocols for One Node
sections.content:
A node using Mobile IPv4 (RFC 3344) keeps connectivity while moving between IPv4 subnets, and a node using Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) does the same for IPv6 subnets. One way to migrate to IPv6 is to deploy dual stack nodes that are both IPv4 and IPv6 capable and can talk to the current IPv4 Internet and to IPv6 networks.

Such a node could use Mobile IPv4 for its IPv4 stack and Mobile IPv6 for its IPv6 stack. The memo says this does not ensure connectivity, because that also depends on the IP version the visited network supports. It is also more inefficient, since mobile nodes must support both protocols and send two sets of signaling messages on every handoff, and administrators must run two sets of mobility management systems.
sections.eli5: It is like keeping two separate address books, one for each kind of phone number, and updating both every time you move house.

sections.title: The Coupling Between Signaling and Address Family
sections.content:
Mobile IP signaling (registration requests in MIPv4, binding updates in MIPv6) sets up tunnels between two end points. Today that signaling is tightly coupled to the address family it manipulates, though the memo sees no fundamental technical reason for this. If Mobile IP were viewed as a tunnel-setup protocol, it should be able to set up IP in IP tunnels whatever the IP version of the outer and inner headers. The memo points out that SIP (RFC 3261) can use either an IPv4 or an IPv6 signaling plane to manipulate IPv4 and IPv6 connections.

A node that is both MIPv4 and MIPv6 capable needs a home agent that supports both protocols, or two separate home agents. It also needs double the configuration in the mobile node and the home agent, such as security associations, and duplicated IP-layer local handover optimizations.
sections.eli5: The two systems are tied to their own kind of address even though they do almost the same job, so one clever system could handle both.

sections.title: The Problems It Causes
sections.content:
The memo lists several specific burdens.

  • Connectivity cannot be guaranteed. A node on an IPv4-only network cannot maintain its IPv6 applications and vice versa. This is described as potentially the most serious problem.
  • Implementation burden. A dual stack node must be capable of both protocols to roam anywhere. A single protocol that handles both IP versions would let a node implement just one, when the protocol choice is known.
  • Operational burden. Operators need deep knowledge of two protocols, and security credentials such as IPsec security associations and keying material are duplicated on mobile nodes and home agents.
  • Signaling inefficiency. On every move the node sends two messages to its home agent, and with local optimizations such as HMIPv6 (RFC 4140) it must update the local agents of each protocol, which costs bandwidth at the critical handover time.

Existing IPv4 to IPv6 transition mechanisms can be combined with Mobile IPv4 or Mobile IPv6, but none are known to help with these issues.
sections.eli5: Doing everything twice wastes time exactly when you are in a hurry, which is while you are moving, and it costs the phone company more work too.

sections.title: Recommended Work Areas
sections.content:
Because Mobile IPv4 is deployed and Mobile IPv6 is expected to be, the memo wants a gradual transition without forcing two protocols to run at once. It says the Mobile IPv6 Working Group considered these work areas reasonable:

  • One mobility management protocol should be able to manage mobility for both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Route optimization for Mobile IPv6 may not be possible in all cases, but mobility management and session continuity can be supported.
  • IPv4 extensions to Mobile IPv6, so a dual stack node can register both home addresses with a dual stack home agent using MIPv6 signaling only.
  • IPv6 extensions to Mobile IPv4, so the same can be done using MIPv4 signaling only.
  • Extensions to both so a node can register a single care-of address, IPv4 or IPv6, to which IPv4 and IPv6 packets can be tunneled.

If the IETF pursues all of these, a vendor could support one protocol and operators could keep one throughout the IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence period. A mobile node would still have to choose one approach or install both. The memo says it introduces no security issues by itself.
sections.eli5: The suggestion is to teach each of the two systems to handle both kinds of addresses, so a phone only needs to learn one.
